$comment: Where each piece of material goes. Written as it is produced, not mined later — the reasoning is freshest the day it is discovered, and a finding nobody routed is a finding nobody uses.

$destinations.landing: A section of the marketing site (docs/WEBSITE-AND-DOCS.md defines the seven).
$destinations.faq: A question a buyer or developer actually asks.
$destinations.docs: A page in the technical documentation.
$destinations.blog: Worth a post of its own — a measured finding with a reproduction that nobody else can publish.
$destinations.internal: Deliberately not published. Needs a reason.

material.what: anon could TRUNCATE every tenant table on a default Supabase project
material.angle: The strongest single artifact keelblock has. It affects every project inheriting Supabase's defaults, RLS does not cover TRUNCATE, and the reproduction is four lines.

material.what: the leading generated RLS suite confirms a total cross-tenant leak as green
material.angle: Why keelblock has two policy layers. The tool is excellent and states its own limit; the demonstration is what makes the argument.

material.what: FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY does not stop the owner on Supabase
material.angle: Corrects advice the tooling itself prints. Narrow, verifiable, useful to anyone on Supabase.

material.what: a cross-tenant write is invisible to the attacker
material.angle: Explains why read-based isolation tests cannot work, in one sentence.

material.what: a failing USING on UPDATE is a silent no-op
material.angle: Shapes every write test anyone writes here.

material.what: Cache Components break every authenticated page in Next 16
material.angle: Anyone adopting Next 16 with auth hits this. The trilemma table is the whole post.

material.what: EXECUTE on a new function defaults to PUBLIC
material.angle: One line in the tenant-table recipe.

material.what: an unconstrained INSERT policy made the access matrix cry wolf
material.angle: Our own defect, and the reason a matrix with a false positive is worse than none.

material.what: an admin could demote the owner and seize the organization
material.angle: Ours. Pairs with F-10 as the argument for auditing a suite you wrote yourself.

material.what: the last owner could orphan an organization
material.angle: Pairs with F-9.

material.what: auth.uid() reads two settings and tools clear only one
material.angle: Too specific to one tool's fixture behavior to be broadly useful; it is documented where it matters, in the gate.

material.what: a deferred constraint trigger is invisible to a statement-level test
material.angle: A correct protection no test can observe is indistinguishable from an absent one.

material.what: keelblock's own unit gate could not fail
material.angle: The most credible thing we can publish, because it is against us. Publishing it is what makes the other twenty-one believable.

material.what: an overclaimed guarantee, corrected
material.angle: Scope note on what the triggers do and do not bind.

material.what: in an app-layer model the other tenant's row is in memory before the check
material.angle: THE explanation of why keelblock exists, and a competitor wrote the code that demonstrates it.

material.what: strict CSP, static prerendering, working hydration — pick two
material.angle: Explains keelblock's report-only default, and is genuinely useful to anyone shipping a CSP on Next.

material.what: NEXT_PUBLIC_ on a credential publishes it, and nothing warns you
material.angle: Short, alarming, true, and no kit examined checks for it.

material.what: keelblock inherited two-majors-behind rot from create-next-app on day two
material.angle: The anti-rot argument, demonstrated on ourselves rather than asserted.

material.what: a gate that misreports its own failure sends you to debug the wrong thing
material.angle: Ours.

material.what: the grep-versus-parse trap, three times, by the person who gated against it
material.angle: Care demonstrably does not work; structure does. The most transferable lesson here.

material.what: a specific date, from an agency blog, in a spec
material.angle: Why the corpus exists. An unverifiable specific is more dangerous than an obvious guess.

material.what: two records of one fact disagreeing, and the gate that hid it
material.angle: Ours.

material.what: documentation that asserts a count is documentation that will lie
material.angle: The durable-versus-volatile rule, and a mechanism for it. This is the one every long-running project needs and almost none has.

material.what: a test that touches shared state is the flake that disables the suite
material.angle: Ours. Short, and the reasoning generalises to any test suite.

material.what: two tracked deferrals silently deleted while every gate said ok
material.angle: A register whose entries nothing references cannot detect its own losses. Generalises to any tracking system, and the failure is invisible by construction.

material.what: the gate protecting keelblock's flagship evidence was indifferent to what the evidence said
material.angle: The strongest self-criticism keelblock has published. A generated artifact needs two guarantees, freshness and content, and guarding only the first proves the document keeps up with the database while saying nothing about whether the database is acceptable. The fix generalizes: adjudication with a published reason, a reason floor so a token cannot retire a leak, and a stale allowance failing so the list cannot rot.

material.what: both anomalies in the published access matrix were false positives, and REACHABLE was a claim the data could not support
material.angle: Grep-versus-parse (F-20) inside a third-party tool, deciding what our own artifact says — plus the distinction between 'this assertion failed' and 'this boundary is open'. The lesson is that the word was kept loud and the dismissals were published with their reproductions, because softening a true signal to accommodate two false ones is how a matrix stops being read.

material.what: a role that could destroy a table it could not read
material.angle: The sequel to F-1 and a sharper version of it: the revoke covered two roles out of three, so service_role kept TRUNCATE on every tenant table and held no DML. Affects every project that copied the F-1 fix. Also the general rule — a hardening statement applied to the objects that existed when it was written decays silently unless ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES carries it forward.

material.what: the committed database types could not be regenerated from the repository
material.angle: A generated artifact is only evidence if it reproduces from the inputs in the repository; this one had recorded a property of one machine — pgTAP's own views, typed as part of the application schema. The failure lands on the newcomer, who is told an artifact is stale through nothing they did. Only a clean rebuild could have found it, because the gate compares the file to whatever the current stack produces.

material.what: the check that certifies every other check was a substring search
material.angle: The sharpest instance of grep-versus-parse this project has: the meta-gate enforcing 'every gate has been shown to fail' did so by looking for a word, which a TODO comment satisfies. Publishable precisely because every proof it guarded turned out to be real — the defect was that nothing could have told us otherwise.

material.what: a guarantee inherited from a platform default is a coincidence with good uptime
material.angle: The single best argument this project can make for its own thesis, and it cost one CI run to find. An assertion green on every local run failed the first time it ran anywhere else, because two builds of the same Supabase Postgres image disagree about what anon may touch. RLS still held; the layer before it did not. The F-1 fix survived the same change because it was written down rather than inherited — same repo, same class, two outcomes, one difference.

material.what: the documentation was falsified by the commit that made it stale
material.angle: The cleanest small illustration of the whole thesis, and self-inflicted: a README sentence was true when written and false for the duration of the push that falsified it. Counts drift slowly and a periodic check catches them; a state claim goes stale instantly, in the same commit as the action. The fix is a badge plus a narrow rule, and the honest note that a project claiming documentation drifts should expect to keep proving it.

material.what: a claim that was true, and a verification that could not have known
material.angle: The sharpest small lesson in the register and it came from an outside reader: a test that passes under both branches of the question it was cited to answer is not evidence for either. SQLSTATE 42501 covers both a missing privilege and an RLS refusal, so the assertion could not confirm which layer refused - and the migration comment presented that breadth as what made the change safe. Being right by accident is not being right.

material.what: an auth cookie is written with cache headers the context cannot apply, and the obvious fix breaks sign-in
material.angle: A cross-USER leak class — one user's session token served to another — in a line of code that looks correct, plus the measurement that stopped us shipping a fix that would have broken sign-in. The reproduction is three lines of output.

material.what: a security property was written down, pinned by a passing test, and not in effect on the running stack
material.angle: The sharpest version of the F-31 lesson, because it is one level up and the test was GREEN. Everyone who edits config and keeps a long-running local stack has this. The reproduction is two shell commands comparing a container start time to a file mtime.

material.what: the session cookie shipped without Secure, and the fix everyone writes breaks sign-in locally with no error
material.angle: Applies to every project on @supabase/ssr, whose DEFAULT_COOKIE_OPTIONS omits `secure` entirely. The NODE_ENV trap is the useful half — `next start` sets production, so the obvious one-liner silently drops every auth cookie over http.

material.what: Next 16.3.4's docs name a testing helper the shipped package does not export
material.angle: Minor on its own; the rule it earns is not. The installed package is the primary source about itself, and documentation describes intent.

material.what: with Cache Components a route cannot refuse with an HTTP redirect — it returns 200 and page chrome
material.angle: Applies to every Next.js app with cacheComponents and a redirect-based auth check, and none of them will notice: the page looks empty and the browser does navigate to sign-in. Four approaches measured, including one that fails the build. The honest half is that we corrected our own spec's wording rather than the measurement.

material.what: a 429 throttle was reported to the user as 'a sign-in link is on its way', for the whole life of the feature
material.angle: The argument for the journey layer in one defect: three green test layers could not see it, and the first browser walk found it immediately. Also a precise correction to a real security practice — anti-enumeration requires hiding whether an account exists, not hiding that the provider refused.

material.what: a boolean helper returned NULL for a non-member — correct in every policy that used it, and silently wrong the first time it was used in an `if`
material.angle: The sharpest illustration of why two test layers exist. In a policy USING clause Postgres reads NULL as a refusal, so the helper was right where it was used and no isolation test could see it; the generated prober mocks these helpers to true/false, so it structurally cannot observe what the real one returns. It took an acceptance test written before the function, in the first procedural caller, to surface a mint into an organization the caller had no membership in. Generalizes to any Postgres codebase with is_… helpers built on a nullable lookup rather than exists().

material.what: the exhaustive RLS prober covered one table while the gate reported three, because the gate counted exit codes instead of files
material.angle: Self-inflicted, in the gate this project points at when it says isolation is proven rather than asserted — which is exactly why it is worth publishing. Each per-table invocation reconciled away the previous one's output, and --no-fail returns zero, so nothing failed. The lesson is the repository's own recurring one in its most expensive location: a check that cannot fail is indistinguishable from a check that passes, and the fix was to compare the claim against the directory. Ships with five mutation proofs, one replaying the exact one-file directory the defect produced.

material.what: the no-test-ids rule pushed page objects onto roles, which collided with Next's route announcer — and the collision was a race that every local run won and the first CI run lost
material.angle: Two things worth publishing. A good rule (accessible locators, no test ids) has a cost nobody warns you about: the framework also ships elements with roles, and `role="alert"` is one of them. And a green local run can be evidence of a faster machine rather than of correct code — the announcer mounts after hydration, so the assertion was racing it. Measuring instead of inferring then turned up an unrelated accessibility defect: two new components created their live region at the same moment as its message, which is the shape that never announces.

material.what: the check that certifies every other check enumerated them by filename, exempting the two rule-enforcing scripts that were not named `check-*` — and when pointed at them, its strictness rule condemned three working proofs
material.angle: The sequel to F-41 and the more useful half: the fix for a check that counts attempts is to ask what it PRODUCED, and the question generalizes to every counting rule in a codebase. Also the counter-lesson nobody publishes — a false positive in a strictness check is worse than a gap, because the repair it demands is rewriting correct code. The rule said three mutation proofs exercised nothing; they went through a one-line helper. Believing it would have meant damaging working tests to satisfy a rule that was itself too narrow.

material.what: the same test-versus-navigation race as F-42, in a different file, surfaced by CI on a documentation-only commit
material.angle: The recurrence is what makes it publishable: once is bad luck, twice is a class. The rule that falls out is sharper than 'add a wait' — when the page is going to navigate, assert on the RESPONSE, not the DOM, because a response body is a fixed artifact and the DOM is a moving one. Also a second data point for the uncomfortable half of F-42: a green local run can be evidence of a faster machine rather than of correct code.

material.what: the upgrade path's central assumption — that a new migration file always applies however far a project has diverged — was false the first time it was tested
material.angle: The category's deepest problem, attacked with a real experiment rather than a claim, and the claim lost. `supabase migration up` refuses a fix whose version sorts before the buyer's own later work, which is the ORDINARY case. Publishable because the correction is small and the reasoning error was total, and because two further things broke that nobody predicts: a second checkout silently shares the first one's database (so the experiment nearly proved a fix had arrived when it was already there), and a generated artifact cannot be shipped by an upgrade at all — upstream's copy describes upstream's schema, and the buyer has tables upstream has never heard of.

material.what: the acceptance bar for upgradability and the ADR describing the upgrade policy contradicted each other, and it only showed up when someone satisfied the bar literally
material.angle: Two documents both written carefully, both reasonable, mutually unsatisfiable: the ADR promises selective adoption of security fixes, the bar demands the current suite pass — and the current suite tests features a selective adopter does not have. The resolution is a genuine design position worth stating: schema is cumulative and adopted whole, product code is the buyer's and is never touched. Schema is cheap to accept and expensive to skip; product code is the reverse.

material.what: the guide for the task where people leak data taught the exact defect a gate had learned to catch hours earlier
material.angle: A gate catching a defect is not the same as the defect being unlearned. The schema guard learned about missing FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY the same day, from a real table that shipped without it — and the flagship guide teaching people to write those tables was not read, so it would have kept teaching it. Measured rather than reasoned: a table built exactly as the guide said reports RLS forced? false, and separately has no grant at all, so it is also unreachable. One gap fails open and one fails closed, which is a useful pair.

material.what: the CI job proving the upgrade path could pass while delivering nothing — and the bar had already been claimed on it
material.angle: The sharpest instance of the recurring lesson, because the author had already written the rule that catches this exact shape. checkPositiveControls exists because a suite of nothing but denials is green against an empty database; the upgrade job was a job whose every step was satisfied by absence. Writing the rule did not stop the same hole being built into the next thing. A lesson learned in one place does not transfer by itself — which is an argument for gates over understanding, made against its own author.

material.what: nothing in the gate suite runs `next build`, so a build-only failure appears as "the web server did not start"
material.angle: Found by an unfamiliar participant in half an hour, and invisible from inside for weeks. The mechanism is the interesting part: the only build in the repository happens inside Playwright's webServer, so its failure mode is disguised as infrastructure. Recorded rather than fixed, because adding the slowest possible step to a gate suite whose count is a stated ceiling is a decision, and a trial's job is to find rather than to choose.

material.what: the fix for a documentation defect introduced a documentation defect, and the next reader concluded the opposite of the truth
material.angle: A correction written in the same breath as the thing it corrects describes the old state in the present tense, because its author holds both versions in mind and the reader only ever sees one. Caught because an unfamiliar participant read the page as written and reported the recipe was wrong — right about the passage, wrong about the code, which is exactly what a misleading document produces. The repair is to date the claim rather than point at "above".

material.what: the default build and the webpack build do not check the same thing, and the default one's page validator cannot fail on props
material.angle: Answering an honest `unknown` produced a premise correction rather than a fix. The pattern two pages use is fine under the build we run and an error under the one we do not; the mechanism is that Turbopack emits a shape constraint where webpack emits an exhaustive one, and the shape constraint types its props as `& any`, which collapses to `any`. Measured, not read: a page declaring a non-Promise, wrongly-named params builds clean. The follow-on is that `next typegen` emits a byte-identical validator, so the gate suite already performed every route-type check the build performs — the reason to add a build had to be found somewhere else.

material.what: thirteen green steps over a page that throws on render, because no step rendered a page
material.angle: The cheapest possible mutation — one `throw` in a page component — separates `tsc --noEmit` (exit 0, silent) from `next build` (exit 1, names the file and the line). A suite can be extensive and still have a whole class outside it, and the way to find out is to break something rather than to reason about coverage. The decision that followed was made on measured numbers: +10.8s median against a 52s loop, no new database prerequisite, and no cost to a gate ceiling that counts rules rather than steps.

material.what: an adversary planted a one-word privilege escalation and every one of the fourteen steps stayed green
material.angle: The trial a harness author cannot run on themselves, run anyway and reported honestly. Three blind spots had to coincide and did: the schema guard read WITH CHECK and never USING, the exhaustive prober mocks the very helpers that ARE the access control, and no test touched project DELETE. The better half is the two near-misses — defects invisible to all three gates that still failed to leak, one because PostgreSQL re-applies SELECT and INSERT policies to a row-moving UPDATE and one because a trigger caught the cascade. The schema survived on defence in depth nobody had credited, which is simultaneously reassuring about the database and damning about the gates.

material.what: the artifact that proves the central claim was reporting a mock on its most important row, and four published cells were wrong
material.angle: A document that says of itself that it describes what the database does, and did not — for the one identity a buyer actually asks about. The mechanism is the exhaustive prober's mocked helpers, so the row reported what a mock admits rather than what a member can do. The larger loss was the guarantee built on it: a matrix that cannot see an authority change cannot make that change appear in review, which is the entire argument for committing it. Fixed by measuring a real member, and the fix promptly produced its own defect — attempts sharing one transaction, so a successful DELETE destroyed the row the later SELECT measured. Found by trying the mutation rather than reasoning about it.

material.what: the login page told users there was no password to leak, and three HTTP requests showed there was
material.angle: A review asked which of two documents was stale and expected an hour of paperwork. Measuring first turned it into a defect: password sign-up and the password grant both work through the publishable key, so a security claim on the first screen a user sees was simply false — and no configuration key can make it true, because Supabase does not expose one. The durable lesson is that copy arguing a position is a claim like any other, and this one was checkable in three requests that nobody had run. Also records a claim the same review offered about a competitor that did NOT survive checking, which is the honest half of taking review input.

material.what: a module was actually deleted to find out what removability costs, and the gates turned out to be most of the test
material.angle: The loudest complaint about starter kits is that you cannot get anything out of them. Rather than argue, the invitations subsystem was deleted and the whole loop run: typecheck, build and 500 tests stayed green, and the four gates that failed each named exactly one leftover until it was gone. Removal took five files across three modules and no archaeology, because the checklist was generated. Also names the two things a deletion test still has to decide — retiring the spec that owns the module, and the fact that a migration cannot be un-run, so removability here is a code property. Includes the author's own first measurement, which was wrong for being broader than the experiment.

material.what: two green CI jobs each proved half of the same story, and nothing crossed between them
material.angle: F-41, F-48, F-49 and F-53 share one shape — components proven, composition unrun — so the shape was pointed FORWARD at a seam nobody had looked at: one job proved a worktree could be upgraded, another proved a generated project checks green, and neither proved a generated project could be upgraded. The prediction was that it would fail. It did not, and that is the cheaper outcome and still worth the ten minutes, because the other one was a defect a buyer finds first. Closed by making one job consume the other's output rather than by adding a third job.

material.what: a gate's verdict depended on the machine running it, and passed locally for that reason
material.angle: The gate already refused a glob because 'a glob is a description, not a path'. An absolute path is the same category error and was not refused, so a criterion citing /tmp/stranger passed on the laptop where a rehearsal had just created that directory and failed on a clean runner. The fix refuses before the existence check, because a rule that only works when the file is missing fixes nothing — and it was swept first: 119 cited paths across every spec, none of this shape, so the rule lands without turning the gate red on real rows.

material.what: three deferrals are waiting on a release process that no spec owns, each keyed to the nearest spec with Release in its title
material.angle: A trigger that fires on an adjacent event is worse than one that never fires and admits it: a spurious fire spends attention and teaches the reader to wave the next one through. Reading the spec rather than its title settled it — the release-preflight spec is the BUYER's deployment gate and mentions publishing nowhere. Two of the three rows were mine and are corrected; the third reasons explicitly to the opposite conclusion and is left alone with its root recorded, because rewriting someone else's considered choice on a draft spec is the over-reach.

material.what: passkeys were promised in two customer-facing documents and owned by no spec or deferral, and the README still advertised the password surface an ADR had just refused
material.angle: The promises gate enforces the acceptance-bar TABLE and cannot enforce the capability list beside it, because that list is prose and the gate refuses to parse prose in its own comments. So the bars were checked, the capabilities were not, and the gap was one word inside a parenthesis. The publishable half is the second instance: the README advertised password sign-in on the same day an ADR refused it and a build gate began failing any module that called signInWithPassword — the code was enforcing the opposite of the marketing.

material.what: a spec said no deferrals were filed while three were armed to fire the moment it closed, and its sibling spec already carried exactly that warning
material.angle: A review read a spec dependency off a column headed ADRs. The correction is more interesting than the error: the dependency graph this build evaluates lives in deferral TRIGGERS, not the spec index, and three rows key on the billing spec — so finishing it turns the build red three ways. The defect was the spec saying "none filed yet", which answers a different question from "none waiting". The sharpest part is that the convention already existed and had been applied to the auth spec in those exact words; a convention applied once and not to its sibling is harder to see than one never invented, because the reader who checks one place finds it there and stops.

material.what: the requirement declaring "no REQ without an AC" had five rules, three implementations and a done acceptance criterion
material.angle: Found by trying to write the missing acceptance criterion for a requirement the owner had just decided. SPEC-003 REQ-7 lists five traceability rules in one sentence; AC-7 was marked done and cited three proofs, and nobody had asked which of the five sentences had code behind them. Three requirements across the set were uncovered, and npm run status could not show it because it counts REQs and ACs separately — 8 REQ, 0/8 AC, one requirement with none and another with two. A count that reads as coverage. The publishable part is the near-miss: the second rule fired on a real row that was correct, because REQ-1..4 is a range, and a false positive on a correct row is how a gate gets exempted into uselessness.

material.what: the sign-in provider button rendered its own translation key, on a spec marked done, because the environment variable that makes the button exist had never been set by anyone
material.angle: The cleanest instance in the whole review of components proven and composition unrun — and the reason the composition never ran is that it was gated behind an environment variable nobody had set. NEXT_PUBLIC_OAUTH_PROVIDERS is empty by default, and that default is CORRECT: a provider button that always fails because no client id exists is worse than no button. So the right default is what kept the surface unreachable, and the answer is not to change it but to render the surface somewhere that is not production. The gate half is F-62's shape again: three structural locale checks all PASS over t('continueWith') against "Continue with {provider}" — the key exists, it is used, there is one locale — and next-intl then refuses to format a message with an unfilled placeholder and returns the key path. The gate checked that the link exists, not that it works. Writing the fourth rule produced two smaller findings against itself, both kept: it first missed object shorthand, failing against the very call site it was written for, and its own docblock quoting t('continueWith', { provider }) was scraped by check 2 as a use of a key that does not exist.

material.what: the whole app stopped hydrating in development because next dev refuses its own HMR and client runtime to 127.0.0.1, and the only visible symptom was one dead button
material.angle: Reported as "the provider button does not respond to clicks"; the code was correct and reading it found nothing. React was never hydrating on ANY page. Nothing throws, every chunk returns 200, and the browser shows only a failed WebSocket — the cause is one line in the dev-server log the browser never sees. The publishable mechanism is why an app-wide failure presented as a single button: a Server Action form posts NATIVELY without JavaScript, so the email form kept working the entire time and progressive enhancement, doing exactly its job, hid that JavaScript was dead. The part that makes it ours rather than the framework's is that keelblock is what sends people to 127.0.0.1 — supabase status prints it, the OAuth redirect URIs are registered against it — so following our own instructions is what breaks development. And it was the SECOND sighting: docs/TESTING.md already recorded a trial losing an afternoon to the same cause, named exactly, found only by reading the dev-server log, and written down as a story about that trial rather than as a fix or a line of config. An observation recorded as narrative is not a fix.

material.what: five of the repository's gates reported violations against documentation that was explaining them, and a sixth had already bent its own prose to avoid one of those false positives rather than filing it
material.angle: Found by taking the defect F-64 produced against its own docblock and asking which other gates share it — then probing each one with realistic documentation instead of reading for the flaw. Four fixed, one deliberately not. The publishable core is the sixth gate: check-policies reads TAP output rather than .sql files and explains that it refuses to enumerate two TAP directive spellings because doing so 'would put a debt-marker word in a file the deferral linter reads'. Somebody hit the false positive, understood it exactly, steered their prose around it, and recorded the workaround instead of the defect — the F-65 shape, one document over. The two silent gates are the better half of the finding because neither is careful: both read something already structured (an AST, an execution log) and never see source text at all. The refusal is the other half: check-deferrals is left broken on purpose, because its markers live in comments by design and narrowing the matcher to silence prose buys a quiet gate at the price of a missed TODO — loud and wrong is the safer failure for a debt linter. And the fix itself nearly went the wrong way: the obvious comment-stripping regex treats the '/*' inside a string literal as a comment opening and blanks real code, trading a loud false positive for a silent false negative. The general shape is that a gate is a reader, and a reader that cannot tell a quotation from a statement will eventually correct the dictionary — four of them made documenting a rule cost you a failing build, which is the exact incentive that leaves rules undocumented.

material.what: adopting shadcn silently killed dark mode across every surface, and the ADR that had measured dark mode working contained no mechanism that could notice
material.angle: shadcn init ships a CLASS-based dark variant, set by a theme toggle it assumes you have; ADR-018 had explicitly refused that toggle with reasons. Nothing set .dark, so all 36 dark: variants across 13 files were dead on arrival — and the failure is silent in every layer that exists: a variant that never matches is not an error, so the CSS compiled, the build passed, typecheck passed, all 575 tests passed, and the page rendered in the light palette on a machine set to dark. Proven from the compiled stylesheet rather than the source, because the source was what was already believed correct. The durable half is that ADR-018 was exactly the kind of entry the previous review asked about — if this recurred tomorrow, what goes red? — and the answer was nothing; it found its first casualty within one session of the question being raised, without the sweep being run, which is the argument for running it. Plus a coda: the test forbidding shadcn's class selector failed on the stylesheet comment written to explain why that selector is refused — F-66's exact shape in a third medium, in the commit that fixed the other two.

material.what: five knip exemptions had outlived the expiry written in their own row, and knip had been printing that fact under Configuration hints on every single run
material.angle: Found by trying to ADD two exemptions and hitting a shrink-only ratchet, which is the ratchet working. The exemption table is well designed — every row carries a 'Removed when' column and the header says an exemption with no expiry is how dead code becomes permanent while looking supervised — and five rows were past their own stated condition: SPEC-004 had shipped, .dom.test.tsx files existed. The ratchet could not have caught it, because it caps how many exemptions exist and says nothing about whether any individual one still earns its place; a count is not coverage. The publishable core is that knip had been answering the question on every run in a channel nobody reads: the exit code was load-bearing and stdout was decoration, and the answer had been sitting in the decoration for weeks. A tool that reports in two channels will be believed in only one of them. Fixed by removing the five, tightening the ratchet 13 to 10, and wrapping knip so a 'Remove from' hint is a build failure while structural hints deliberately are not.

material.what: keelblock's own site has no owning spec, and the gate that routes findings to a blog proves only that a destination was named, not that anything was ever published
material.angle: Found by being handed the wrong home for the proof page — and the document that says it is the wrong home was already in the repository, stating both of its own gaps in advance. The publishable half is the gate reading as coverage: check-content reports how many findings are routed and to where, and not one has been published anywhere; the number is accurate and the sentence it forms is false. Deliberately NOT gated, and the reasoning is the useful part — the obvious rule fails on every such row the day it lands, which ADR-023 forbids, and the weaker rule that passes today is vacuous until publishing starts, which is F-13. So the fix is a spec claiming the document, not a gate. Third instance this session of the sweep's thesis: noticing is where the work stops, and a document that names its own gap reads as diligence right up until the gap costs something.

material.what: an open redirect in the auth callback, an application rendering in the browser default serif, and environment validation that executed in no process — none visible to twelve green gates
material.angle: The strongest thing this project can publish and the most uncomfortable. A genuinely external review found three defects in shipped code; all three were re-derived by execution before anything was changed. The open redirect is the technically sharp one: the origin check was not wrong, it was asked of the wrong thing — new URL normalises '/..' away leaving a protocol-relative PATHNAME, so the input genuinely resolved on-origin and the RETURN VALUE was the payload. The file's own docblock already contained the fix ('a blocklist is a list of the payloads someone thought of') and had applied that rule to the input only. Its old test ended with an INVARIANT under a comment saying a list is always the set someone thought of, and then iterated a list of eight; a generated property test finds 251 escaping inputs against the old function. The serif is the honest one and it was self-inflicted by the shadcn commit — and the reported one-line fix was necessary and not sufficient, which only surfaced by rendering the page: the token was correct and still out of SCOPE, defined on body and consumed at html. The unifying sentence is the publishable one: every gate asks whether a claim is true, none asks whether the product works. An open redirect is a correct function with the wrong argument, a serif page is valid CSS, a validator nobody calls is a passing unit test.

material.what: the local CI verifier ignored working-directory, so it would have run `supabase db reset` against the developer's own database while printing that it was executing exactly as CI does
material.angle: The design is right — parse the workflow and execute its steps, because a hand-written local mimic drifts. It dropped one key, and the key mattered: a step CI runs inside a throwaway /tmp/scaffold would have run in the repository root and dropped every table in the developer's own database. The publishable sentence is that a fidelity claim wrong in the destructive direction is worse than no fidelity claim: every other honesty mechanism in that file is careful — four states, skips named with reasons, a printed percentage genuinely executed — and the percentage counted a step running in the wrong place as faithful. Fixed by honouring the key, by reporting the step as skipped-with-a-reason when the directory is absent (the file's own fourth state, not a new concept), and by adding a destructive entry to a list whose stated purpose was 'slow OR destructive' and had none. The test plans every step of the REAL workflow rather than a fixture, because a fixture would have been right while the workflow was wrong.

material.what: the invitation journey dead-ended because the login screen never read the destination both server actions were already built to accept
material.angle: Defect family A at journey scale. invite/[token] links to /login?next=/invite/<token>; requestMagicLink already read a next field off its FormData and startOAuth already took a next argument; the page never read the parameter, the form never submitted it, and the button called the action with one argument. Every part correct, the composition missing — the same shape as the OAuth button that rendered its own translation key, except the assembly here is a JOURNEY, the thing a person is actually trying to do, and a journey has no failing test when one link is missing unless somebody walks it. Fixed on both paths deliberately: a journey that survives one and not the other fails half the time. Walked in a browser rather than asserted, because the previous three defects passed every test in the repository.

material.what: the scaffolder's headline command crashed, and the second and third defects behind it appeared only after the first was fixed and the command was run again
material.angle: npx create-keelblock-app is the single sentence a new user is most likely to type, and it built `git clone --branch HEAD`, which git refuses because --branch takes a branch or a tag and HEAD is neither. The publishable mechanic is the layering: with the clone fixed, the same run died on `ls-tree null`, and with that fixed an end-to-end assertion found every generated project shipping an empty docs/review/ directory. Reading found one; running found two; asserting found three. The reason CI could not catch any of it is exact and reusable — the scaffold job always passes --ref "$GITHUB_SHA", so the default invocation is the one combination CI never exercises, and it is the only one a user types. Every defect in that file lives in the ~90 lines of main() that no test executes.

material.what: the commit that corrected an overclaimed label missed the file a new reader opens first, leaving a correction and its contradiction two files apart
material.angle: docs/review/ was labelled an external review; it is a session the owner ran, and DEF-020 already drew that line — 'a session the author spawned is not one'. The correction landed in README.md and missed HANDOVER.md and ADR-015. F-60's class occurring inside the fix for itself, which is the argument for making it a rule instead of a third correction: a test now fails if any reader-facing document describes the folder as external, and reports the file and line. Small, but it is the cleanest available example of why a one-time correction is not a mechanism.

$differentiators: Every spec that ships a competitive capability, written up the day it ships. A spec that is done or partial declares what it lets keelblock claim, what the field does instead, evidence that resolves, and a battlecard section that exists — or is listed in $noDifferentiator with a reason. Checked by scripts/check-content.mjs. This exists because SPEC-004's Server-Action rule shipped and routed nowhere: the findings pipeline keys on F-* ids, and a capability produces none by itself, so the gap could only be noticed by a person saying it out loud.

differentiators.claim: Tenant isolation is enforced by row-level security, so a foreign tenant's row is never selected — there is no second step to forget.
differentiators.rivals: BoxyHQ, the most-starred free kit in the category, isolates in application code: getApiKeyById fetches any tenant's row by id, and a separate guard the route must remember to call compares the tenant afterwards. Zero `create policy` statements across their schema.
differentiators.battlecard: Isolation is a database property, not an application convention
differentiators.oneLine: _Every kit tells you it isolates tenants. Ask which layer refuses, and what

differentiators.claim: Isolation is proven per table, per command, per identity, and the resulting access matrix is committed and regenerated byte-for-byte in CI.
differentiators.rivals: Nobody in the field publishes isolation proof. MakerKit has some tests, Supastarter journey e2e, ShipFast none — and none publishes a matrix of who can read and write what, per role, per table.
differentiators.battlecard: The proof is published, and it can fail
differentiators.oneLine: _A test suite that cannot fail is a screenshot. Ask to see the mutation

differentiators.claim: Values that are correct by default are pinned anyway, so a vendor changing a default is a failing build rather than a silent loss of a security property.
differentiators.rivals: The field ships the generated config and inherits whatever the vendor chose. Every project inheriting Supabase's defaults inherits sessions that never expire and a password floor below the vendor's own recommendation.
differentiators.battlecard: A security property that is inherited is not a property
differentiators.oneLine: _Ask which of their security properties are true because someone chose

differentiators.claim: Every exported Server Action reaches an authorization call — resolved through the module graph, per action — or is declared public with a written reason, and the build refuses one that does neither.
differentiators.rivals: Nothing in the category checks this. Next.js documents the exposure itself: an exported action is reachable by direct POST even if never imported, and a page-level check does not extend to it. Its own mitigations are described as reducing risk where an auth layer is missing, not as a boundary.
differentiators.battlecard: Every Server Action authorizes, and the build refuses one that does not
differentiators.oneLine: _Your Server Actions are public POST endpoints. Ask what happens when

differentiators.claim: The organization switcher is a view selection, not a security boundary — policies ask the database per request whether the caller is a member, so a forged or stale active organization returns nothing rather than someone else's rows.
differentiators.rivals: The common design puts the active organization in the session or a JWT claim and has policies read it back, which makes the switcher part of the boundary and inherits a token's staleness: an access token lives up to an hour, so a revoked admin stays an admin until it turns over. Supabase's own RBAC guide recommends that pattern and never mentions the window.
differentiators.battlecard: A switcher that is allowed to be wrong
differentiators.oneLine: *Ask what their organization switcher does when it is wrong — and how long a revoked admin keeps their access.*

differentiators.claim: A removed member loses access on their very next request, not when their token expires — proven by a browser journey that fails if the removal is skipped. And the one row a stranger must read is exposed through a single function returning a named two-column type, not a policy that admits anon.
differentiators.rivals: The usual invitation surface is a policy admitting `anon` plus an application-side filter on the token, which selects the row before deciding the caller was entitled to it — and the usual membership check is a JWT claim, which cannot be revoked before it expires. Supabase's own RBAC guide recommends the claim pattern and does not mention the window; its default access token lives up to an hour.
differentiators.oneLine: *Ask them to remove a signed-in teammate while you watch, and time how long the access lasts.*

differentiators.claim: The upgrade path is tested rather than described: which files an upgrade may take is a list in code with a mutation proof that it never touches product code, and the strategy's own load-bearing assumption was measured false the first time a synthetic buyer was upgraded — and corrected in the ADR rather than worked around.
differentiators.rivals: MakerKit documents `git pull upstream main` and its page does not mention merge conflicts. supastarter's own documentation states that updating "will become harder" with every change you make to your application, because you are rebasing your code onto theirs. Neither publishes a test that an upgrade works, and neither addresses what happens to generated artifacts that describe the buyer's schema rather than the vendor's.
differentiators.battlecard: An upgrade path that was tested before it was claimed
differentiators.oneLine: *Ask what happens when they fix a security bug and you cloned in March — then ask to see the test.*

differentiators.claim: The repository's teachability is measured rather than asserted: an unfamiliar participant is given one feature task and no help, and what the gates failed to catch is published as a finding.
differentiators.rivals: Every kit in the category asserts its documentation is good and none publishes a trial. The measurement is cheap and nobody runs it, so no competitor can tell you what a newcomer got wrong in their repository last week — or what their own checks stayed silent about.
differentiators.battlecard: A handover trial that publishes what it missed
differentiators.oneLine: *Ask when they last watched somebody fail to use their documentation, and what that person got wrong.*

differentiators.claim: A generated project records the release and commit it came from and keeps the remote that makes those objects reachable, so it can take a later release. The five-minute claim is a CI job with a budget rather than a number in a README.
differentiators.rivals: degit sells discarding history as the feature — it downloads a tarball "because you're not downloading the entire git history". create-next-app initialises a fresh repository by default (--disable-git turns it off) and its CLI reference gives no upgrade guidance for a generated project at all. Read 2026-09-09; the claim is only as broad as the documentation actually opened, and does not speak for kits whose docs were not.
differentiators.battlecard: A generated project that can still take a security fix
differentiators.oneLine: _Ask what your generated project remembers about where it came from. Usually nothing — and that is why there is no upgrade._

differentiators.claim: The getting-started page is executed on every push — its shell blocks extracted and run in one shell in an empty directory, asserting that a real project came out rather than that the commands exited zero.
differentiators.rivals: boxyhq/saas-starter-kit has one CI workflow and every step in it runs an npm script; no step executes their installation documentation. Read 2026-09-09, and the claim is exactly as broad as that one file — it says nothing about the paid kits, whose CI is not public.
differentiators.battlecard: A setup page that was known to work on this commit
differentiators.oneLine: _Ask when their setup page last worked. Ours answers with a commit, because a job follows it._

$noDocumentation.SPEC-003: The gates document themselves at the point of failure: every one names the file, the line and the fix, and AGENTS.md carries the table of what each catches. A separate page describing them would be a second copy that goes stale the first time a message is improved.
$noDocumentation.SPEC-006: Covered by CONTRIBUTING.md's authoring recipes and by the invitation flow being the product surface itself. Revisit when the first task guide for invitations exists — a stranger inviting a teammate follows the UI, not a page.
